name: City Centre and Nachlaot
tagline: Around Machane Yehuda, where the market becomes the nightlife
description: The area around Jaffa Road, the light rail and the Machane Yehuda market, with the dense old lanes of Nachlaot beside it. The market's stalls close in the evening and the bars behind their shutters open, which is the city's best night out. Central, walkable and expensive.
bestFor: Anyone who wants the market, the bars and the light rail on the doorstep
pros: Machane Yehuda market and its bars a few minutes away
Light rail through the middle of it
The most walkable part of the city
cons: Among the highest rents in a very expensive city
Noisy, and completely shut from Friday afternoon

name: German Colony and Baka
tagline: Stone houses and Emek Refaim, the quietest central address
description: The southern districts built by German Templers in the nineteenth century, with stone houses, gardens and the cafes and restaurants of Emek Refaim street. It is the most comfortable part of Jerusalem to live in, popular with English-speaking residents, and priced accordingly.
bestFor: Longer stays wanting quiet stone streets and the largest English-speaking community
pros: Cafes and restaurants along Emek Refaim
cons: The most expensive residential district in the city
Twenty-five minutes on foot to the Old City

name: Old City
tagline: Inside the walls, four quarters in one square kilometre
description: The walled city holding the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Al-Aqsa compound within a few hundred metres of each other, divided into Jewish, Muslim, Christian and Armenian quarters. Living here means stone lanes, no vehicles, and being inside the most contested square kilometre on earth.
bestFor: Short stays where being inside the walls is the entire point
pros: The three faiths' central sites within a short walk
Extraordinary atmosphere, particularly early and late
cons: Security incidents and access restrictions are a recurring reality
Crowds and no vehicle access for deliveries

name: Rehavia and Talbiya
tagline: The 1930s Bauhaus quarter near the government buildings
description: The central residential districts west of the old city, built in the 1930s in a restrained modernist style, with tree-lined streets, the Prime Minister's residence and a short walk to the centre. It is settled, professional and among the most desirable addresses in Jerusalem.
bestFor: Stays wanting a quiet professional district within walking distance of everything
pros: Ten minutes on foot to the city centre
Close to the national institutions and museums
cons: Quiet, with little nightlife of its own
Heavy security presence around some streets

name: Givat Ram and the University Side
tagline: Around the Hebrew University campus and the museums
description: The western institutional district holding the Hebrew University's Givat Ram campus, the Israel Museum with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Knesset and the Bible Lands Museum. Student housing and academic accommodation make it the most affordable central option, and the Jerusalem Forest is on the western edge.
bestFor: Anyone connected to the university, with the museums a short walk away
pros: University facilities and the Israel Museum nearby
The most affordable central housing, through the university
Jerusalem Forest on the western edge for running
cons: Institutional and quiet in the evenings
Twenty minutes from the city centre
Housing largely tied to academic status
